No. When working overseas you must use a company‑managed device with the approved VPN; personal laptops and other non‑managed devices must not be used to access company systems. Access may also be restricted by destination country, network, role, or system, and you must not access from restricted locations [HR-POL-005 §4.5; HR-POL-005 §8; HR-POL-004 §10.4].

If you’re traveling, arrange a company‑managed device and confirm your destination isn’t restricted. If you’re unsure, contact Information Security for guidance.

Short answer: No. You can raise a concern in good faith without having to prove the complete case first [HR-POL-011 §4.4 Good-faith reporting].

Key points
- Good-faith reports are allowed even if you don’t have complete evidence. Knowingly false or malicious allegations are not allowed, but an unsubstantiated concern is not automatically malicious [HR-POL-011 §4.4 Good-faith reporting].
- Sensitive matters (harassment, discrimination, retaliation, threats, violence) should be escalated through People and Culture/the formal channel [HR-POL-001 §4.2 Respectful and secure work; HR-POL-011 §8 Decision Rules].
- Retaliation is prohibited when someone raises a concern in good faith [HR-POL-011 §8 Decision Rules].
- If immediate safety is at risk, prioritize safety and emergency support first [HR-POL-011 §8 Decision Rules].

Practical steps
- When you report, share what happened, when/where, who was involved, and any supporting details you have. Preserve any relevant messages or files.
- If you tell a manager, they should preserve information, avoid promising outcomes, and contact People and Culture; they must not discuss it unnecessarily or change your work adversely because you raised the concern [HR-POL-011 §5.4 Initial response by managers].

If you’d like, I can outline how to contact People and Culture via the formal channel for your location.

Here’s what applies for a six‑week overseas work request with company‑systems access:

- Duration limit and exceptions
  - Standard limit is 30 calendar days in any rolling 12 months; six weeks exceeds this and is not compliant under the ordinary pathway. An exception requires formal executive review after manager, People and Culture, Information Security, and location‑risk assessments [HR-POL-004 §4.4].
- Approvals and timing
  - Submit the request at least 20 calendar days before departure; shorter notice needs documented justification [HR-POL-004 §5.2].
  - Written approval from the manager and People and Culture is required before booking travel; approval is effective only after all required reviews are documented [HR-POL-004 §5.3].
- Destination and location risk
  - You must not work from a destination classified as restricted (e.g., confidentiality, connectivity, sanctions, tax/immigration, employment‑location, insurance, or personal‑safety concerns) [HR-POL-004 §4.5; HR-POL-012 §2].
- Accessing company systems overseas
  - Use a company‑managed device and the approved VPN; access may be restricted by country, network, data type, role, or system. Do not access from restricted destinations [HR-POL-005 §4.5; §8].
  - Prefer trusted private networks. Public/shared Wi‑Fi may be used for confidential work only if the approved VPN is active and you can prevent visual/overheard disclosure. Do not bypass network controls [HR-POL-005 §4.4].
  - If a device is lost or you suspect a security incident, report within one hour where personal safety permits [HR-POL-005 §8].

If you share the destination country and planned dates, I can point you to the next steps for the location‑risk and security reviews.

Here’s what applies for a six‑week overseas work request with company‑systems access:

- Duration limit and exceptions
  - Standard limit is 30 calendar days in any rolling 12 months; six weeks exceeds this and is not compliant under the ordinary pathway. An exception requires formal executive review after manager, People and Culture, Information Security, and location‑risk assessments [HR-POL-004 §4.4].
- Approvals and timing
  - Submit the request at least 20 calendar days before departure; shorter notice needs documented justification [HR-POL-004 §5.2].
  - Written approval from the manager and People and Culture is required before booking travel; approval is effective only after all required reviews are documented [HR-POL-004 §5.3].
- Destination and location risk
  - You must not work from a destination classified as restricted (e.g., confidentiality, connectivity, sanctions, tax/immigration, employment‑location, insurance, or personal‑safety concerns) [HR-POL-004 §4.5; HR-POL-012 §2].
- Accessing company systems overseas
  - Use a company‑managed device and the approved VPN; access may be restricted by country, network, data type, role, or system. Do not access from restricted destinations [HR-POL-005 §4.5; §8].
  - Prefer trusted private networks. Public/shared Wi‑Fi may be used for confidential work only if the approved VPN is active and you can prevent visual/overheard disclosure. Do not bypass network controls [HR-POL-005 §4.4].
  - If a device is lost or you suspect a security incident, report within one hour where personal safety permits [HR-POL-005 §8].

If you share the destination country and planned dates, I can point you to the next steps for the location‑risk and security reviews.

Short answer: No. If a recognized public holiday for your assigned location falls during your approved PTO on a day you would ordinarily work, that day is treated as a public holiday and should not be deducted from your PTO. I’m sorry this happened. Here’s what to do next, based on company policy:

- Report it immediately. A lost device is a security incident and must be reported within one hour of discovery where safe to do so [HR-POL-005 §5.4]. Loss or theft is handled under the incident-reporting process in the Equipment Policy [HR-POL-009 §5.2].

items.answer:
Here’s how to handle a sensitive workplace complaint and any related HR case, grounded in company policy:

- Prioritize immediate safety. If there is any threat or risk of harm, focus on safety and emergency support first, then notify People & Culture (P&C) promptly [HR-POL-011 §8].
- Escalate through the formal channel. Concerns involving harassment, discrimination, retaliation, threats, or significant security risk must be referred to People & Culture without delay [HR-POL-001 §4.2; HR-POL-011 §8].
- Do not adjudicate. Do not try to determine who is right or wrong or resolve the facts through automated guidance; this belongs with HR/P&C [HR-POL-011 §8].
- Protect confidentiality; share only what’s necessary. Collect and transmit the minimum information needed to enable HR to act, and involve People & Culture where sensitive details are required [HR-POL-010 §4.2; HR-POL-001 §4.2].
- Gather essential facts accurately. Focus on what happened, when/where, who was involved, any witnesses, and any urgent needs or safety concerns—avoid unnecessary personal or medical details [HR-POL-010 §4.2; HR-POL-001 §4.3].
- Emphasize anti-retaliation. Make clear that anyone raising a concern in good faith must not face retaliation, and escalate any retaliation concerns immediately [HR-POL-011 §4.2; HR-POL-011 §8].
- Handle records carefully. Use authorized company systems, protect confidential information, and restrict access to those with a need to know; do not store sensitive case details in shared or informal channels [HR-POL-001 §4.2; HR-POL-010 §4.2].
- Communicate supportively and neutrally. Acknowledge the concern, explain that HR/P&C will manage intake and investigation, and avoid promises about outcomes or timelines [HR-POL-011 §8].

If you’d like, I can help you draft a report to People & Culture summarizing the concern (only the essential facts).
